steps.title: Put each one in the correct column.
Four sentences from a story about a jump from 38 kilometres.
steps.sub: Notice the form of each verb.

items.text: He jumped out of the capsule.
He didn’t think about the view.

steps.title: Look at the four sentences again.
steps.sub: He jumped · He fell · He didn’t think · When did it open?
steps.prompt: What happens to the verb after didn’t and did?
options: It goes back to its base form.
It keeps the -ed ending.
It takes an -s.
steps.answer: It goes back to its base form.
steps.why: The past is already in did: didn’t think, did it open — not didn’t thought.

steps.title: Past Simple
steps.html:
Regular verbIrregular verb
+He jumped out of the capsule.He fell too fast.
–He didn’t land on his feet.He didn’t think about the view.
?Did he jump at 5.37?Did his parachute open?
short answerYes, he did.No, he didn’t.
was / wereThe team was worried.Eight million people were watching.

Regular verbs add -ed: jump → jumped, land → landed, watch → watched. After -e add only -d: dive → dived.

Irregular verbs change: fall → fell, go → went, take → took, buy → bought, tell → told. There is no rule — learn them.

Negatives and questions use did + the base form for every verb, regular or irregular.

Be is the exception: was / were, with no did: He was safe. Were you frightened?

In the next lesson you will put the Past Simple next to the Past Continuous.

steps.title: Ten minutes under the snow
steps.sub: One snowboarder, ten minutes, one brother.
steps.html:
Reading

I started snowboarding when I was fifteen, and for nine years nothing went wrong.

Then, in February, my brother and I took a lift to the top of a small mountain above our town. The weather changed while we were putting our boots on, but we did not think about it. We dropped over the edge together and rode down through the trees.

I remember the noise. It came from behind me, and it was not loud — it sounded like a train a long way off. Then the snow lifted me up, turned me round and round, and pulled me down.

When I stopped, everything was dark. I could not move my arms. I did not fall far, but I was under the snow and I did not know which way was up. So I spat, and I watched the water run down my face. That told me where the ground was. I dug towards my feet, then backwards, then forwards again, and after two or three minutes I got one hand out.

My brother did not see me stop. He rode on for four hundred metres, then turned round and climbed back up. He called the rescue team from the middle of the slope, and they arrived in eleven minutes. They pulled me out, and one of them gave me hot tea and asked me my name three times.

I did not go back that season. But in December I bought a new board.

People ask me if it was frightening. It was — but not at the time. At the time I was busy.

steps.title: Choose the best answer.
options: A snowboarder who was caught under the snow and rescued.
A snowboarder who broke a world record.
A brother who taught the writer to snowboard.
steps.answer: A snowboarder who was caught under the snow and rescued.
steps.why: The snow buried the writer; the brother called the rescue team.
